---
title: "R and Bioconductor"
engine: knitr
---


::: {.objectives}
**After working through this chapter you will be able to**

- explain where R's design makes statistical and genomic work shorter than the equivalent Python, and where it does not
- predict the result of R's recycling and coercion rules instead of discovering them in a wrong answer
- diagnose the three errors factors cause, and convert a factor to its labels safely
- subset a data frame in base R and with dplyr, and read both idioms in other people's code
- reshape a count matrix between wide and long form, and build a ggplot2 figure one layer at a time
- construct `Biostrings`, `GRanges` and `SummarizedExperiment` objects from bundled data and say what each class guarantees
- assemble a `SummarizedExperiment` in which sample annotation cannot become detached from its counts
:::

R was written by statisticians, for statistics, and it shows in every corner of the language. There is no scalar type: a single number is a vector of length one. Missing data has its own value, `NA`, which propagates through arithmetic instead of quietly becoming zero. A linear model, a *t*-test and a false discovery rate correction are in the base installation, not in a package. None of that is an accident, and none of it is how Python works. The consequence for bioinformatics is that a great deal of what you want to do with a count matrix, a table of variants or a set of genomic intervals is one line in R and a loop in most other languages.

The second reason to learn R is Bioconductor: a coordinated collection of more than two thousand packages, released twice a year as a tested set, built on shared data structures for sequences, genomic intervals and assay matrices. Almost every published RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, methylation and microarray analysis of the last twenty years passed through it. You cannot work in genomics for long without meeting a `GRanges` object or a `SummarizedExperiment`, and once you can read those two classes most Bioconductor documentation becomes intelligible.

This chapter uses five bundled datasets. The RNA interference experiment of @brooks2011 supplies a count matrix of 14,599 *Drosophila* genes across seven samples (`data/expression/pasilla_gene_counts.tsv`) and its sample annotation (`data/expression/pasilla_sample_annotation.csv`); these carry the data-handling, reshaping and plotting sections, and the `SummarizedExperiment` you build at the end is the object the RNA-seq chapter uses for its DESeq2 analysis. The *Mycoplasmoides genitalium* G37 genome (`data/sequences/mycoplasma-genitalium-NC_000908.2.fasta`) and its RefSeq annotation (`data/annotation/mycoplasma-genitalium.gff`) carry `Biostrings` and `GRanges`, and the eight p53 orthologues in `data/proteins/p53-orthologs.fasta` give a protein sequence set to work on.

The Python chapter covered some of this ground in another language, and this one does not repeat it. Where the two differ in how they think — about vectors, about missing values, about where metadata lives — the difference is the lesson.

## Why R, and where it wins {#sec-07-why-r}

R is an open implementation of the S language, which was designed at Bell Laboratories for interactive data analysis [@rcoreteam]. Three features of that design matter daily.

**Everything is a vector.** `length(3.14)` is 1. Arithmetic, comparison and most functions operate on whole vectors at once, so the loop you would write in another language is usually absent in R. That is not merely cosmetic: a loop you do not write is a loop whose index you cannot get wrong.

**Statistics is in the language, not bolted on.** `t.test`, `lm`, `p.adjust`, `quantile` and the full family of probability distributions ship with R. When an analysis reaches the point of needing a *p*-value, there is nothing to install.

**Packages are a first-class concern.** CRAN holds over twenty thousand packages, each required to pass automated checks on several platforms before release; Bioconductor adds a biological layer on top with its own, stricter, review and a twice-yearly coordinated release.

Where R loses is equally worth knowing. It is slower than Python for text processing and for explicit loops, it has no equivalent of Biopython's parsers for the long tail of file formats, and its tooling for general software engineering is thinner. The honest division of labour is that pipelines and parsers tend to be written in Python and in shell, and the statistical analysis of what they produce tends to be written in R.

Every R chapter of this book opens with the same setup, which makes the bundled data reachable and sets the plotting style.

```{r}
#| label: setup-07
source(file.path("..", "R", "_common.R"))
cat(R.version.string, "\n")
```

## Vectors, vectorisation and recycling {#sec-07-vectors}

Read the count matrix with base R first, because the base functions are what you will meet in older scripts and in package source code.

```{r}
#| label: read-counts-base-07
counts_df <- read.delim(book_data("expression", "pasilla_gene_counts.tsv"))
count_matrix <- as.matrix(counts_df[, -1])
rownames(count_matrix) <- counts_df$gene_id

dim(count_matrix)
count_matrix[1:3, 1:4]
```

`read.delim` returns a data frame; dropping the first column with `[, -1]` and calling `as.matrix` gives a numeric matrix, and the gene identifiers move from a column to the row names. A matrix holds one type of value, which is what allows `colSums` and friends to be fast.

A row of that matrix is a named numeric vector, and most of what you want to know about it is a single function call.

```{r}
#| label: vector-basics-07
pasilla_gene <- count_matrix["FBgn0000008", ]
pasilla_gene
c(mean = mean(pasilla_gene), sd = sd(pasilla_gene), median = median(pasilla_gene))
```

**Vectorisation** means an operation applies to every element without a loop. Comparison returns a logical vector, and logical vectors are how you select.

```{r}
#| label: vectorisation-07
pasilla_gene > 100
names(which(pasilla_gene > 100))
sum(pasilla_gene > 100)
```

`sum` on a logical vector counts the `TRUE` values, because `TRUE` becomes 1 when a numeric answer is required. That is **coercion**, R's rule for mixing types: a vector holds one type, so combining types silently promotes everything to the most general one, in the order logical → integer → double → character. `c(1, 2, "three")` is a character vector in which the `1` is now the text `"1"`. A column of counts arriving as character because one spreadsheet cell said `not done` is this rule in action, and the symptom is arithmetic refusing to work on data that looks numeric.

Normalising counts to counts per million exposes the second rule, **recycling**: when two vectors of different lengths meet, R repeats the shorter one until it matches the longer.

```{r}
#| label: recycling-07
c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60) / c(1, 2)
library_size <- colSums(count_matrix)
library_size
```

Recycling is convenient when the short vector has length one — `count_matrix / 1000` divides everything by 1,000 — and dangerous otherwise. Dividing the whole matrix by the vector of library sizes looks correct and is not.

```{r}
#| label: recycling-trap-07
wrong_cpm <- 1e6 * count_matrix / library_size
right_cpm <- 1e6 * t(t(count_matrix) / library_size)

round(wrong_cpm["FBgn0000008", ], 2)
round(right_cpm["FBgn0000008", ], 2)
round(colSums(right_cpm))
```

A matrix in R is a vector with a dimension attribute, filled column by column, so dividing it by a length-7 vector recycles that vector *down the rows*, not across the columns. Each count is divided by whichever library size happens to land on it. The result is numerically plausible — all seven values are small positive numbers of the right order of magnitude, and one of them, `untreated3`, is even correct by coincidence — which is exactly why this is a dangerous bug rather than an obvious one. Transposing twice, as `right_cpm` does, aligns the vector with the columns; the check that proves it is that every column of the corrected matrix now sums to exactly one million.

Missing values follow their own rule. `NA` is contagious: any arithmetic involving it returns `NA`, so that a missing measurement cannot be silently treated as zero.

```{r}
#| label: missing-values-07
measurements <- c(12, 7, NA, 31)
mean(measurements)
mean(measurements, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(is.na(measurements))
```

The design decision is deliberate, and it is one of the places R is clearly better than a language in which a missing value becomes an empty string or a zero. If you want the mean of what you have, you must say so with `na.rm = TRUE`, and saying so is a decision recorded in the code.

## Factors, and the trouble they cause {#sec-07-factors}

A **factor** is R's type for a categorical variable: it stores the data as integer codes plus a table of **levels**, the permitted categories. Statistical functions need this — `lm` and `t.test` must know that `treated` and `untreated` are two levels of one variable rather than two arbitrary strings — and the level order sets the reference category, which decides the sign of every coefficient a model reports.

```{r}
#| label: factors-07
condition <- factor(c("untreated", "treated", "treated", "untreated"))
condition
levels(condition)
as.integer(condition)
```

The levels came out in alphabetical order, so `treated` is the reference and a model fitted on this variable would report changes *relative to the treated samples* — the opposite of what the experiment means. Set the order explicitly whenever it matters.

```{r}
#| label: relevel-07
condition <- factor(c("untreated", "treated", "treated", "untreated"),
                    levels = c("untreated", "treated"))
levels(condition)
```

Three failure modes follow from the integer-plus-levels design, and all three appear in real analyses.

```{r}
#| label: factor-traps-07
lane_counts <- factor(c("5", "2", "2", "2", "6", "2", "2"))
as.numeric(lane_counts)
as.numeric(as.character(lane_counts))

treated_only <- condition[condition == "treated"]
table(treated_only)
table(droplevels(treated_only))
```

The first trap is the serious one: `as.numeric` on a factor returns the internal codes, not the labels, so a column of lane counts converted this way becomes a different set of numbers with no error anywhere. The route through `as.character` is the only safe one. The second trap is that subsetting keeps levels that no longer occur, so `table` reports a category with zero members and `ggplot2` draws an empty box for it; `droplevels` removes them. The third is that combining two factors with different levels works on the integer codes rather than the labels, so convert to character, combine, and re-factor.

::: {.callout-warning title="A factor is not its labels"}
Before R 4.0, `read.csv` turned every character column into a factor by default, and a decade of analyses carry bugs from it. The default is now `stringsAsFactors = FALSE`, so modern code gets character columns — but data read with older code, loaded from an `.RData` file, or returned by a package that still converts, may be factors. When a numeric column behaves strangely, check `class()` before anything else, and convert with `as.numeric(as.character(x))`, never `as.numeric(x)`.
:::

## Data frames, tibbles and two ways to subset {#sec-07-data-frames}

A **data frame** is a list of equal-length vectors presented as a table, so each column has its own type. It is the structure almost all R analysis passes through. A **tibble** is the tidyverse's data frame: the same thing with three behaviours changed, all of them to remove surprises [@wickham2019].

```{r}
#| label: read-annotation-07
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

samples <- read_csv(book_data("expression", "pasilla_sample_annotation.csv"),
                    show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  rename(lanes = `number of lanes`, exon_counts = `exon counts`) |>
  mutate(sample = sub("fb$", "", file), .before = 1) |>
  select(sample, condition, type, lanes, exon_counts)

samples
```

The sample names in the annotation file carry an `fb` suffix that the count matrix columns do not; `sub` strips it so the two tables can be joined. That mismatch is typical, and noticing it early is the difference between a join that works and a join that silently returns nothing.

Printing shows the first differences. A tibble reports its dimensions and the type of every column, and prints ten rows rather than every row. The deeper differences appear when you subset.

```{r}
#| label: tibble-vs-dataframe-07
samples_df <- as.data.frame(samples)

class(samples_df[, "condition"])   # a data frame drops to a vector
class(samples[, "condition"])      # a tibble stays a tibble
samples_df$cond[1:3]               # partial matching: $ finds "condition"
```

A data frame with one column selected returns a vector, which breaks any code downstream that expected a table; a tibble always returns a tibble, and `samples$condition` or `samples[["condition"]]` is how you ask for the vector. And `$` on a data frame matches partially, so a typo such as `samples_df$cond` returns the `condition` column instead of `NULL`. On a tibble it returns `NULL` with a warning, which is the behaviour you want: a mistyped column name should be an error, not a silent substitution.

Base R and dplyr express the same selection differently, and you need to read both, because thirty years of published R code uses the first idiom.

```{r}
#| label: subsetting-side-by-side-07
# base R: rows by logical vector, columns by name, inside one [ ]
samples_df[samples_df$condition == "treated" & samples_df$lanes == 2,
           c("sample", "type", "exon_counts")]

# dplyr: one verb per operation, chained
samples |>
  filter(condition == "treated", lanes == 2) |>
  select(sample, type, exon_counts)
```

The results are identical; the difference is where the complexity sits. Base R's `[` does two jobs at once and requires you to repeat the name of the data frame inside the condition, which is where typos hide. dplyr splits the work into verbs, evaluates column names inside the data, and reads left to right. For interactive analysis the second is easier to get right; for package code the first has the advantage of depending on nothing.

## Verbs, pipes and tidy data {#sec-07-dplyr}

dplyr provides a small set of verbs that each do one thing: `filter` chooses rows, `select` chooses columns, `mutate` adds or changes columns, `arrange` sorts, `summarise` collapses, and `group_by` makes the verb after it work within groups. The native pipe `|>` passes the value on its left into the first argument of the call on its right, so a chain of verbs reads as a sentence.

```{r}
#| label: dplyr-verbs-07
samples |>
  mutate(counts_per_lane = exon_counts / lanes) |>
  group_by(condition, type) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_per_lane = mean(counts_per_lane), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(mean_per_lane))
```

Four groups, one line each: the design is unbalanced, with a single treated single-read library and two of everything else. That imbalance is the chapter's recurring theme and it matters for the analysis in the RNA-seq chapter, because library type is partly confounded with condition.

::: {.callout-note title="Two pipes, and which to use"}
R has two pipes. The magrittr pipe `%>%`, which the tidyverse introduced, is a function from a package and allows a `.` placeholder: `x %>% f(y, .)`. The native pipe `|>` has been part of base R since version 4.1, needs no package, and always passes into the first argument. Use `|>` in new code — it works in a script with no libraries attached, and it is what current tidyverse documentation uses — and expect to meet `%>%` in everything written before about 2022.
:::

### Tidy data and pivoting

Data is **tidy** when each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each type of observational unit is a table. The count matrix is not tidy: its seven columns are not seven variables but seven values of one variable, `sample`. Wide form is the right shape for matrix algebra and for every Bioconductor assay class; long form is the right shape for `ggplot2` and for `group_by`. Converting between them is the most common single operation in a tidyverse analysis.

```{r}
#| label: pivot-longer-07
library(tidyr)

long_counts <- read_tsv(book_data("expression", "pasilla_gene_counts.tsv"),
                        show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  pivot_longer(-gene_id, names_to = "sample", values_to = "count") |>
  left_join(samples, by = "sample")

dim(long_counts)
head(long_counts, 3)
```

`pivot_longer(-gene_id, ...)` means "pivot every column except `gene_id`", turning 14,599 rows by 7 columns into 102,193 rows of three. The `left_join` then attaches the annotation by matching the `sample` column in both tables — which only works because the `fb` suffix was stripped earlier.

With the data long, a per-sample summary is one grouped `summarise`.

```{r}
#| label: library-summary-07
library_summary <- long_counts |>
  group_by(sample, condition, type) |>
  summarise(library_size = sum(count), genes_detected = sum(count > 0),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(library_size)

library_summary
```

The four paired-end libraries are the four smallest, between 8.4 and 10.3 million counts, and the three single-read libraries are the three largest, between 14.0 and 21.9 million. Library size and library type are not independent in this experiment, and neither is independent of condition. `pivot_wider` reverses the operation when a matrix is needed again, and running it on `long_counts` reproduces the original table exactly — a check worth making the first few times you pivot anything.

## The grammar of graphics {#sec-07-ggplot}

`ggplot2` is not a collection of plot types. It is an implementation of a grammar: a plot is a dataset, a mapping from variables to **aesthetics** (position, colour, shape, size), one or more **geometries** that draw the mapped data, **scales** that control how a variable becomes an aesthetic, optional **facets** that split the plot into panels, and a **theme** that governs everything carrying no data. Each of those is added with `+`, and a plot can be stored in a variable and extended later. Building one figure in stages is the fastest way to see what each layer does.

Start with the data and a mapping, and add the simplest geometry.

```{r}
#| label: fig-07-counts-raw
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of non-zero gene counts in each pasilla sample, drawn on a linear scale. Each box is a sample; the points are the values ggplot2 classifies as outliers. The plot is unreadable because the counts span five orders of magnitude."
library(ggplot2)

expressed <- long_counts |> filter(count > 0)
counts_plot <- ggplot(expressed, aes(x = sample, y = count))
counts_plot + geom_boxplot()
```

@fig-07-counts-raw is a useful failure. The boxes are flattened onto the axis and the only visible feature is a column of outliers, because gene counts run from 1 to over 300,000 and a linear axis gives almost all of its height to the few thousand genes above 50,000. Nothing about the comparison between samples is legible. The fault is not the geometry — a boxplot is the right summary here — but the **scale**.

Add a logarithmic scale, and map condition to the fill aesthetic so that the two groups are distinguishable.

```{r}
#| label: fig-07-counts-scaled
#| fig-cap: "The same distributions on a log scale, with colour mapped to experimental condition. Changing one scale makes the comparison between samples legible; the default colour palette has not yet been changed."
scaled_plot <- counts_plot +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = condition)) +
  scale_y_log10()
scaled_plot
```

@fig-07-counts-scaled is the same data and the same geometry, with one scale changed, and it now shows a real pattern: the medians differ between samples by about a factor of two, and the differences do not line up with the colours. Treated and untreated samples are interleaved, which means the largest visible source of variation is not the treatment. Note also what the aesthetic mapping did — `fill = condition` was placed inside `aes()`, because the colour is determined *by a variable*. A fixed colour that carries no information goes outside `aes()`, as a plain argument.

The last stage adds facets, the book palette and labels. Faceting by library type is a hypothesis: if library preparation explains the pattern, the panels will be internally consistent.

```{r}
#| label: fig-07-counts-final
#| fig-cap: "Non-zero gene counts per sample, faceted by library preparation type and coloured by condition. Within each panel the four distributions are closely matched; between panels the medians differ by roughly a factor of two, which identifies library type rather than treatment as the dominant source of variation."
final_plot <- scaled_plot +
  facet_grid(. ~ type, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = book_palette[c(2, 1)]) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Counts per gene (log scale)", fill = NULL,
       title = "Library type dominates the count distributions") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
final_plot
```

@fig-07-counts-final answers the question. The paired-end libraries have medians near 150 to 200 counts and the single-read libraries near 260 to 340, and within each panel treated and untreated samples sit on top of one another. A difference between the panels that is larger than the difference between the colours is the visual signature of a batch effect, and it is why the differential expression model in the RNA-seq chapter includes library type as a term rather than ignoring it. Adding a second `scale_y_log10()` also demonstrates a detail of the grammar: when two scales for the same aesthetic are added, the later one replaces the earlier rather than combining with it.

Three habits make `ggplot2` easier. Keep the data long, because every aesthetic must map to a column. Store the plot in an object and add to it, so that experiments cost one line. And remember that `theme()` controls only what carries no data — fonts, grid lines, legend position — so to change what a plot *says* you need a different aesthetic, geometry or scale, not a theme.

## Iteration and functions {#sec-07-iteration}

R's answer to "do this to every column" is a family of functions that take a function as an argument. `apply` works over the rows or columns of a matrix, `sapply` and `lapply` over the elements of a list or vector, and `vapply` does what `sapply` does while requiring you to state the type of the result, which turns a class of silent failures into errors.

```{r}
#| label: apply-family-07
head(round(rowMeans(count_matrix), 2), 3)
apply(count_matrix, 2, median)
vapply(as.data.frame(count_matrix), function(x) sum(x == 0), integer(1))
```

Prefer the specialised functions where they exist: `rowMeans`, `colSums`, `rowSums` and `colMeans` are implemented in C and are much faster than `apply` on a large matrix. Reach for `apply` only when there is no specialised version, as for `median`.

The `purrr` package covers the same ground with a consistent interface and type-stable variants — `map_dbl` always returns a double vector, `map_int` an integer vector, `map` a list — and a compact formula notation in which `.x` is the current element.

```{r}
#| label: purrr-07
library(purrr)

map_dbl(as.data.frame(count_matrix), ~ sum(.x) / 1e6) |> round(2)
```

A real use of iteration: test every well-expressed gene for a difference between conditions. Filtering first is not optional — a gene seen a handful of times carries no information and costs multiple-testing power.

```{r}
#| label: per-gene-tests-07
keep <- rowSums(count_matrix >= 10) >= 3
log_cpm <- log2(right_cpm[keep, ] + 1)
groups <- samples$condition[match(colnames(log_cpm), samples$sample)]

p_values <- apply(log_cpm, 1, function(gene) t.test(gene ~ groups)$p.value)
q_values <- p.adjust(p_values, method = "BH")

c(tested = length(p_values),
  raw_below_0.05 = sum(p_values < 0.05),
  bh_below_0.05 = sum(q_values < 0.05))
```

Of 14,599 genes, 8,148 pass the expression filter. Of those, 1,547 have an uncorrected *p*-value below 0.05 — but roughly 407 would be expected by chance alone at that threshold, so the raw count is close to uninterpretable. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure [@benjamini1995], one call to a base R function, controls the expected proportion of false discoveries among the genes called significant and leaves 195. The analysis is deliberately naive: a *t*-test on log counts per million ignores the mean–variance relationship of count data, which is what DESeq2 [@love2014] and edgeR [@robinson2010] model, and the RNA-seq chapter redoes it properly. It is here because three lines took a 14,599-gene matrix from raw counts to a corrected result.

### Writing functions

A function in R is a value like any other. The body's last expression is the return value, arguments may have defaults, and defaults may refer to other arguments.

```{r}
#| label: write-function-07
counts_per_million <- function(count_column, library_size = sum(count_column)) {
  if (!is.numeric(count_column)) {
    stop("count_column must be numeric", call. = FALSE)
  }
  1e6 * count_column / library_size
}

round(counts_per_million(count_matrix[, "untreated1"])[1:3], 3)
tryCatch(counts_per_million(letters), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

The input check is the part most often left out and the part that saves the most time. Without it, passing a character vector produces an error from deep inside the arithmetic, far from the mistake; with it, the message names the argument.

### When non-standard evaluation bites

dplyr lets you write `filter(samples, condition == "treated")` without quoting `condition`, because the verbs capture the expression and evaluate it inside the data rather than in the calling environment. This is **non-standard evaluation**, and it is pleasant until you try to write a function around it.

```{r}
#| label: nse-failure-07
summarise_by_broken <- function(data, group_column) {
  data |>
    group_by(group_column) |>
    summarise(observations = n(), .groups = "drop")
}

tryCatch(summarise_by_broken(long_counts, condition),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

The error is exact: dplyr looked for a column literally called `group_column`. The fix is to **embrace** the argument with `{{ }}`, which tells dplyr to substitute what the caller passed before evaluating.

```{r}
#| label: nse-fixed-07
summarise_by <- function(data, group_column) {
  data |>
    group_by({{ group_column }}) |>
    summarise(observations = n(), total_counts = sum(count), .groups = "drop")
}

summarise_by(long_counts, condition)
summarise_by(long_counts, type)
```

One pair of braces turns a function that cannot work into one that works for any grouping column. This is the single most common point at which people who are fluent in interactive dplyr get stuck when they start writing functions, and the symptom — an error naming your own argument as a missing column — is distinctive enough to recognise immediately.

## Bioconductor {#sec-07-bioconductor}

Bioconductor began in 2001 with a practical problem: every microarray group was writing its own code to attach probe identifiers to measurements, and none of it was interoperable [@gentleman2004]. The answer was to define shared classes and require packages to use them, so that the output of one package is the input of the next. Three commitments follow, and they explain most of what looks unusual about Bioconductor code.

Packages use **S4 classes**, a formal object system with declared slots and validity checking, rather than the looser S3 system of base R. You access parts of an object through **accessor functions** — `assay()`, `colData()`, `seqnames()` — rather than reaching into slots with `$` or `@`. And the whole collection is released twice a year as a tested set, with every package checked against every other, which is why a Bioconductor version number is a meaningful statement about an analysis [@huber2015].

### Installing with BiocManager

Bioconductor packages are not installed with `install.packages`. The `BiocManager` package resolves the correct package versions for your release.

```{r}
#| label: bioc-install-07
#| eval: false
install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install(c("Biostrings", "GenomicRanges", "rtracklayer",
                       "SummarizedExperiment"))
BiocManager::valid()
```

Those commands reach CRAN and the Bioconductor repositories, so they are not run
when this book is built. The output below was captured from a real run of
`BiocManager::version()` and `BiocManager::valid()` in the environment this
chapter was written in, abridged where the report lists individual packages.

```
[1] '3.20'

Bioconductor version '3.20'

  * 17 packages out-of-date
  * 0 packages too new

create a valid installation with

  BiocManager::install(c(
    "BH", "BiocParallel", "Biostrings", "GenomeInfoDb", "IRanges",
    "MatrixGenerics", "RCurl", "SparseArray", "callr", "colorspace", "curl",
    "edgeR", "lambda.r", "limma", "restfulr", "selectr", "tinytex"
  ), update = TRUE, ask = FALSE, force = TRUE)
```

`BiocManager::valid()` is the command worth remembering: it reports any installed package that is out of step with your Bioconductor release, which is the usual cause of an error message that makes no sense.

::: {.callout-note title="Record the Bioconductor version, not just the package version"}
A Bioconductor release pins a set of mutually tested package versions to one R version. Stating "Bioconductor 3.20 under R 4.4" in a methods section identifies the software far more precisely than a list of individual package versions, and `BiocManager::version()` returns it in one call. Annotation packages change between releases as the underlying databases are rebuilt, so a result can shift when only the annotation has moved.
:::

### Biostrings

`Biostrings` stores sequences in a compressed representation that holds a whole genome in a fraction of the memory a character vector would need, and provides the operations the alphabet implies [@lawrence2013]. Attach the Bioconductor packages now; note that they mask a few base and dplyr names, which is why they are loaded after the tidyverse work is done.

```{r}
#| label: biostrings-load-07
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(Biostrings)
  library(GenomicRanges)
  library(rtracklayer)
  library(SummarizedExperiment)
})

genome <- readDNAStringSet(book_data("sequences",
                                     "mycoplasma-genitalium-NC_000908.2.fasta"))
genome
```

```{r}
#| label: biostrings-composition-07
letterFrequency(genome, c("G", "C", "A", "T"))
round(100 * letterFrequency(genome, "GC", as.prob = TRUE), 2)

chromosome <- genome[[1]]
subseq(chromosome, 1, 48)
reverseComplement(subseq(chromosome, 1, 48))
```

A `DNAStringSet` is a set of sequences; `[[` takes one out as a `DNAString`. The GC content of 31.69% is low even for a reduced bacterial genome, and it has a direct consequence for the codon usage and oligonucleotide composition you can measure in the same two lines.

```{r}
#| label: biostrings-patterns-07
head(sort(oligonucleotideFrequency(chromosome, 3), decreasing = TRUE), 5)
countPattern("TTTAAA", chromosome)
length(matchPattern("GGAGG", chromosome))
```

The five commonest trinucleotides are all A or T only, as a 31.7% GC genome requires. `matchPattern` returns the positions of every match of the Shine–Dalgarno-like `GGAGG` motif, not merely the count. Protein sequences use the parallel class.

```{r}
#| label: biostrings-proteins-07
orthologs <- readAAStringSet(book_data("proteins", "p53-orthologs.fasta"))
width(orthologs)
head(sort(alphabetFrequency(orthologs[[1]])[1:20], decreasing = TRUE), 4)
```

The eight p53 orthologues range from 352 to 393 residues [@uniprot2023], and the human protein's commonest residues are proline, serine, glycine and alanine — consistent with the large intrinsically disordered regions at both ends of p53.

### GRanges and genomic intervals

Half of genomics is interval arithmetic: which variants fall in which genes, which peaks overlap which promoters, how much of a genome is annotated. `GenomicRanges` provides `GRanges`, a vector of intervals each with a sequence name, start, end and strand, plus arbitrary metadata columns, and `rtracklayer` reads GFF3, GTF, BED and BigWig into it [@lawrence2013].

```{r}
#| label: granges-import-07
annotation <- import(book_data("annotation", "mycoplasma-genitalium.gff"))
class(annotation)
table(annotation$type)
```

The file is the RefSeq annotation produced by NCBI's prokaryotic pipeline [@tatusova2016]. Keep the gene features and the three metadata columns worth carrying, then declare the sequence length, which is what lets `GRanges` refuse an interval running off the end of the chromosome.

```{r}
#| label: granges-genes-07
genes <- annotation[annotation$type == "gene"]
mcols(genes) <- mcols(genes)[, c("locus_tag", "gene", "gene_biotype")]
seqlengths(genes) <- 580076

genes[1:3]
summary(width(genes))
```

Now a real overlap computation. In a genome this compact, adjacent genes are expected to abut and sometimes to overlap, because the intergenic regions have been eroded. `findOverlaps` answers the question directly, returning every pair of indices whose intervals share at least one base; keeping only pairs where the first index is smaller removes self-matches and the duplicate of each pair.

```{r}
#| label: granges-overlaps-07
hits <- findOverlaps(genes, genes, ignore.strand = TRUE)
hits <- hits[queryHits(hits) < subjectHits(hits)]
overlap_width <- width(pintersect(genes[queryHits(hits)],
                                  genes[subjectHits(hits)],
                                  ignore.strand = TRUE))

length(hits)
length(unique(c(queryHits(hits), subjectHits(hits))))
summary(overlap_width)
```

189 pairs of annotated genes overlap, involving 300 of the 546 genes — more than half the genome's gene complement. The median overlap is 10 bp and the largest is 113 bp. An overlap of a few bases is the signature of translational coupling, where the stop codon of one gene and the start codon of the next share sequence in an arrangement such as `ATGA`, and it is a well-documented feature of reduced genomes. Without an interval class this would be a nested loop; here it is one call, backed by an interval tree, so it stays fast on a human genome with two million features.

Intervals also answer density questions. `tileGenome` cuts the chromosome into fixed windows and `countOverlaps` counts the features in each, which is the computation behind every coverage track you have ever looked at.

```{r}
#| label: granges-tiles-07
tiles <- tileGenome(seqlengths(genes), tilewidth = 10000,
                    cut.last.tile.in.chrom = TRUE)
tiles <- tiles[width(tiles) == 10000]        # drop the short final window
tiles$n_genes <- countOverlaps(tiles, genes, ignore.strand = TRUE)
summary(tiles$n_genes)
```

@fig-07-gene-density plots that count along the genome. Converting a Bioconductor object for `ggplot2` is a standard move: `as.data.frame` on a `GRanges` gives columns for `seqnames`, `start`, `end`, `width`, `strand` and every metadata column.

```{r}
#| label: fig-07-gene-density
#| fig-cap: "Annotated genes per 10 kb window across the Mycoplasmoides genitalium G37 chromosome. The dashed line is the genome-wide mean of 10.3 genes per window. The sparsest window, at 430-440 kb, contains only five genes because two of them are the 4.2 kb and 3.9 kb RNA polymerase subunits rpoB and rpoC."
gene_density <- as.data.frame(tiles) |>
  dplyr::mutate(midpoint_kb = (start + end) / 2000)

ggplot(gene_density, aes(x = midpoint_kb, y = n_genes)) +
  geom_col(width = 9, fill = book_palette[1]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(gene_density$n_genes),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = book_palette[4]) +
  labs(x = "Genome position (kb)", y = "Genes per 10 kb window",
       title = "Gene density along a reduced bacterial genome")
```

Density varies from five to 21 genes per window around a mean of 10.3, and the variation is almost entirely a matter of gene length rather than of gene-free sequence: the sparsest window holds the two RNA polymerase subunit genes, which between them occupy 8 kb of the 10 kb, while the densest holds 21 protein-coding genes averaging 522 bp. A density track answers the question "how many features per window", which is not the question "how much of this region is functional".

### SummarizedExperiment

A quantitative experiment is three things that must stay aligned: a matrix of measurements, a table describing the columns, and a table describing the rows. Keeping them in three separate variables works until something reorders one of them, at which point every result is wrong and nothing errors. `SummarizedExperiment` is the class that makes that impossible [@huber2015].

The failure it prevents is worth seeing first. The annotation table lists the samples in a different order from the count matrix columns.

```{r}
#| label: se-the-bug-07
samples$sample
colnames(count_matrix)
```

```{r}
#| label: se-the-bug-shown-07
naive <- data.frame(sample = colnames(count_matrix),
                    condition = samples$condition)
naive
```

Six of the seven labels in that table are wrong: three untreated samples are called treated and three treated samples untreated, because a character vector was pasted beside a matrix on the assumption that both were in the same order. A differential expression analysis built on it would run to completion, produce a volcano plot, and be meaningless. It is the commonest serious bug in expression analysis, and no diagnostic plot reveals it.

Build the object properly. The sample table is reordered *by name* to match the matrix columns, and the row annotation is computed from the matrix itself.

```{r}
#| label: se-build-07
sample_table <- samples |>
  tibble::column_to_rownames("sample") |>
  dplyr::mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = c("untreated", "treated")),
                type = factor(type))
sample_table <- sample_table[colnames(count_matrix), ]

gene_table <- DataFrame(total_count = rowSums(count_matrix),
                        detected_in = rowSums(count_matrix > 0),
                        row.names = rownames(count_matrix))

storage.mode(count_matrix) <- "integer"
pasilla_se <- SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = count_matrix),
                                   colData = sample_table,
                                   rowData = gene_table)
pasilla_se
```

The printed summary is the anatomy of the class. `dim` gives features by samples, 14,599 by 7. `assays` lists the matrices — here one, named `counts`, and a second could hold normalised values on the same grid. `rowData` holds one row per gene, `colData` one row per sample, and `metadata` is a free-form list for provenance. The accessors return each part.

```{r}
#| label: se-accessors-07
assay(pasilla_se, "counts")[1:3, 1:4]
colData(pasilla_se)
head(rowData(pasilla_se), 3)
```

The guarantee is that the object cannot be built wrong. Passing sample annotation whose row names do not match the matrix columns is refused outright, and so is a table with the wrong number of rows.

```{r}
#| label: se-refuses-07
shuffled <- sample_table[c(3, 1, 2, 5, 4, 7, 6), ]
tryCatch(SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = count_matrix),
                              colData = shuffled),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))

tryCatch(SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = count_matrix),
                              colData = sample_table[1:6, ]),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Sample order is not metadata"}
The order of columns in a matrix is an accident of how a file was written. Never rely on it. Match sample annotation to measurements by name — `sample_table[colnames(count_matrix), ]` — and put both in one object so the question cannot arise again. It prevents a class of error that no plot will reveal and no reviewer will catch.
:::

From then on the object behaves like a two-dimensional array in which everything moves together. Subsetting rows filters the gene annotation; subsetting columns filters the sample annotation; and `$` reaches into `colData` directly.

```{r}
#| label: se-subset-07
expressed_se <- pasilla_se[rowData(pasilla_se)$detected_in >= 3, ]
paired_se <- expressed_se[, expressed_se$type == "paired-end"]

dim(expressed_se)
dim(paired_se)
as.character(paired_se$condition)
```

```{r}
#| label: se-assays-07
assay(pasilla_se, "cpm") <- 1e6 * t(t(assay(pasilla_se, "counts")) /
                                      colSums(assay(pasilla_se, "counts")))
metadata(pasilla_se) <- list(
  source = "Brooks et al. 2011, GEO GSE18508",
  counted_with = "HTSeq, gene level",
  built_in = "Chapter 7 of Practical Approach to Learning Bioinformatics"
)

assayNames(pasilla_se)
round(assay(pasilla_se, "cpm")["FBgn0000008", ], 2)
```

A second assay sits on the same grid as the first, so a gene selected from one is the same gene in the other. The counts themselves were produced by counting reads per gene with HTSeq [@anders2015htseq], which is the kind of fact the `metadata` slot exists to carry. Saving the object with `saveRDS` writes matrices, both annotation tables and the metadata to one file, and this is the object the RNA-seq chapter loads and hands to DESeq2 — where `DESeqDataSet` is simply a `SummarizedExperiment` with a design formula attached, which is why the hand-over needs no conversion at all. The same holds for most of Bioconductor: `limma` [@ritchie2015] and `edgeR` accept or return the same structure, and a class understood once is understood everywhere.

## Reproducible reporting {#sec-07-reporting}

Everything in this chapter was produced by a document holding both the prose and the code, rendered by Quarto with the `knitr` engine [@xie2015]. The idea is Knuth's literate programming, inverted for data analysis [@knuth1984]: the figures and the numbers in the text cannot disagree with the analysis, because they are generated from it every time the document is built.

A Quarto document is Markdown with executable chunks. Each chunk has options set in `#|` comment lines: a label for cross-referencing, a caption, whether to show the code, whether to run it.

````{.markdown}
```{r}
#| label: fig-07-density-example
#| fig-cap: "Genes per 10 kb window."
#| warning: false
ggplot(gene_density, aes(midpoint_kb, n_genes)) + geom_col()
```
````

Rendering with `quarto render chapter.qmd` runs every chunk in a fresh R session, in document order, and fails if any of them fails. That last property is the one that matters: a document that renders is a document whose code runs from a clean start, which is a guarantee a notebook cannot make.

The remaining piece is a record of the software. `sessionInfo()` reports the R version, the platform and the version of every attached package, and belongs at the end of any analysis document.

```{r}
#| label: session-info-07
session <- sessionInfo()
session$R.version$version.string
head(vapply(session$otherPkgs, function(pkg) pkg$Version, character(1)), 6)
```

Printing `sessionInfo()` on its own gives the full report — operating system, locale and loaded-but-not-attached packages — tedious to read and invaluable when an analysis stops reproducing. Pair it with a pinned environment file, as described in the Unix chapter, so the versions are not merely recorded but restorable [@sandve2013].

## Summary {#sec-07-summary}

- R has no scalars. Operations apply to whole vectors, which removes most loops and, with them, most index errors.
- Recycling repeats the shorter operand silently. On a matrix it recycles down the columns, so dividing a count matrix by a vector of library sizes gives a plausible, wrong answer.
- Coercion promotes mixed types to the most general one, and a factor is integer codes plus labels: a numeric column that will not do arithmetic is almost always character or factor, and only `as.numeric(as.character(x))` recovers a factor's labels.
- Tibbles differ from data frames in the ways that matter for safety: no partial matching, no dropping to a vector, no silent factor conversion.
- Base R subsetting and dplyr verbs express the same operations. Write the second; be able to read the first.
- Tidy data has one variable per column, which is the shape `ggplot2` and `group_by` require, and the opposite of the shape Bioconductor assays require. `pivot_longer` and `pivot_wider` move between them.
- A ggplot is data, aesthetics, geometries, scales, facets and a theme. When a plot is unreadable, change the scale before the geometry.
- Bioconductor's value is its shared classes. `Biostrings` for sequences, `GRanges` for intervals and `SummarizedExperiment` for assay matrices cover most of what a genomics analysis needs to hold.
- Keeping counts, sample annotation and feature annotation in one `SummarizedExperiment` makes the commonest serious bug in expression analysis — a mismatch between samples and their labels — impossible to commit.
- A rendered Quarto document plus `sessionInfo()` is a result that can be rebuilt. A result that cannot be rebuilt is a claim.

## Exercises {#sec-07-exercises}

1. Predict, before running it, what `c(TRUE, 2L, 3.5, "four")` returns and what `class()` reports for it. Then check.
2. Create the factor `factor(c("10", "20", "30"))` and convert it to the numbers 10, 20 and 30. Explain in one sentence what `as.numeric()` alone returns and why.
3. Using `samples`, write one dplyr pipeline that returns the sample name, condition and exon counts for every paired-end library, sorted from largest to smallest. Then write the same selection in base R.
4. Compute the median counts per million of each sample from `right_cpm`, and say which library type has the higher median. Why is this not evidence of a biological difference?
5. Add a `geom_jitter()` layer of 200 randomly chosen genes on top of @fig-07-counts-scaled. What does the layer order tell you about how `ggplot2` draws a plot?
6. Using `matchPattern`, find every occurrence of the start codon `ATG` on the forward strand of the *M. genitalium* chromosome, and compare the count with the 524 annotated coding sequences. Explain the discrepancy.
7. Build a `GRanges` of the transfer RNA genes only (`gene_biotype == "tRNA"`), and use `distanceToNearest` to find how far each one lies from the nearest protein-coding gene. Report the median distance.
8. Write a function `filter_by_detection(se, min_samples)` that returns a `SummarizedExperiment` containing only genes detected in at least `min_samples` samples, and show that the returned object's `colData` is unchanged.
9. The `pasilla_se` object contains one treated single-read library and two treated paired-end libraries. Using `table()` on `colData`, show the design, and explain in two or three sentences why this makes the effect of condition and the effect of library type partly inseparable.

## Solutions {#sec-07-solutions}

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" title="Solutions"}

**1.** Everything is coerced to character, because character is the most general of the four types present.

```{r}
#| label: soln-07-1
mixed <- c(TRUE, 2L, 3.5, "four")
mixed
class(mixed)
```

**2.** `as.numeric()` alone returns 1, 2, 3 — the internal integer codes of the three levels, which happen to be in the same order as the labels here and so look almost right. The safe route converts to character first.

```{r}
#| label: soln-07-2
sizes <- factor(c("10", "20", "30"))
as.numeric(sizes)
as.numeric(as.character(sizes))
```

**3.**

```{r}
#| label: soln-07-3
samples |>
  filter(type == "paired-end") |>
  select(sample, condition, exon_counts) |>
  arrange(desc(exon_counts))

samples_df[order(-samples_df$exon_counts), ][
  samples_df$type[order(-samples_df$exon_counts)] == "paired-end",
  c("sample", "condition", "exon_counts")]
```

The base R version needs the ordering applied twice, once to the rows and once to the vector used in the condition, which is a fair illustration of why the verb form is easier to get right.

**4.** The single-read libraries have the higher median. This is a property of library preparation and sequencing depth, not of biology: counts per million corrects for total depth but not for the different distribution of reads across genes that paired-end and single-read protocols produce, and the two protocols are not randomly assigned to conditions in this experiment.

```{r}
#| label: soln-07-4
median_cpm <- apply(right_cpm, 2, median)
data.frame(median_cpm = round(median_cpm, 3),
           type = samples$type[match(names(median_cpm), samples$sample)])
```

**5.** The jittered points are drawn *on top of* the boxes, because layers are drawn in the order they are added. Adding `geom_jitter()` before `geom_boxplot()` would hide the points behind the boxes.

```{r}
#| label: soln-07-5
set.seed(20250101)
sampled_genes <- dplyr::slice_sample(expressed, n = 200)

scaled_plot +
  geom_jitter(data = sampled_genes, width = 0.2, size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5)
```

**6.** There are far more `ATG` occurrences than coding sequences, because most are internal codons, out of frame, or in the reverse-strand genes, which this search does not see at all.

```{r}
#| label: soln-07-6
atg_hits <- matchPattern("ATG", chromosome)
c(atg_occurrences = length(atg_hits), annotated_cds = 524)
```

Gene finding needs a model of reading frames, ribosome binding sites and codon statistics, which is what Prodigal and the NCBI pipeline provide; counting start codons is not even a first approximation.

**7.**

```{r}
#| label: soln-07-7
trnas <- genes[genes$gene_biotype == "tRNA"]
coding <- genes[genes$gene_biotype == "protein_coding"]
nearest_hits <- distanceToNearest(trnas, coding, ignore.strand = TRUE)

length(trnas)
summary(mcols(nearest_hits)$distance)
```

The median distance is small — a few tens of base pairs — which is another expression of the compactness seen in @fig-07-gene-density.

**8.**

```{r}
#| label: soln-07-8
filter_by_detection <- function(se, min_samples) {
  stopifnot(is(se, "SummarizedExperiment"), min_samples >= 0)
  detected <- rowSums(assay(se, "counts") > 0)
  se[detected >= min_samples, ]
}

filtered <- filter_by_detection(pasilla_se, min_samples = 5)
dim(filtered)
identical(colData(filtered), colData(pasilla_se))
```

`identical` returning `TRUE` is the point: subsetting rows cannot disturb the sample annotation, because the subsetting method is defined on the whole object rather than on the matrix.

**9.**

```{r}
#| label: soln-07-9
table(colData(pasilla_se)$condition, colData(pasilla_se)$type)
```

The design is unbalanced: one treated single-read library against two untreated, and two treated paired-end against two untreated. Because every cell of the table is occupied, library type can be included as a term in a model and its effect estimated — the design is not fully confounded. But with one sample in the smallest cell, the estimate of the single-read effect in treated samples rests on a single library, so a technical oddity in that one library is indistinguishable from a treatment effect specific to single-read preparation. A balanced design with equal numbers in all four cells would have cost nothing extra and removed the ambiguity.

:::

## Further reading {#sec-07-further-reading}

- @wickham2019 is the paper that introduced the tidyverse as a coherent set; read it for the design principles that explain why the verbs are shaped as they are.
- @gentleman2004 is the original Bioconductor paper and is still the clearest statement of why shared classes, rather than shared functions, were the right thing to standardise.
- @huber2015 describes the modern Bioconductor infrastructure, including `SummarizedExperiment`, and is the reference to cite when you use the class.
- @lawrence2013 sets out the range-based classes and the algorithms behind `findOverlaps`; worth reading before you write any interval arithmetic of your own.
- @love2014 is the DESeq2 paper, and its methods section explains why the naive *t*-test in @sec-07-iteration is the wrong model for count data.
- @xie2015 documents `knitr`, the engine that executes the chunks in this book; its chapter on chunk options answers most questions about controlling output.
- @yu2012 is a well-built Bioconductor package to read as code: it takes a gene list and returns an enrichment result, using the shared classes throughout.
- @cock2009 is the Biopython reference, worth comparing with `Biostrings`: the same operations, a different design, and an illustration of how much of a library's shape follows from its host language.
